evidence: docs/manifest-signing.md:22 (added): "On POSIX, rebar refuses a provisioned key file with any group or other permission bit (it must be `0600` or stricter)."

docs/manifest-signing.md:7 and :14 place this section in the context of `rebar sign`, `rebar.sign_manifest`, and the MCP `sign_manifest` tool. docs/manifest-signing.md:20 introduces `REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH` as the general provisioned-key override.

src/rebar/_opcert_signing.py:159-167: the general key resolution reads REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH and only raises when `not os.path.exists(override)`, then returns the path. There is no mode check, and the file has no `0o077` match.
src/rebar/opcert_service/keyprov.py:1-9 and :107-121: the 0600-or-stricter refusal applies only to the op-cert service's startup FILE source in compose_signer/_read_path_source.

docs/README.md:47 catalogs manifest-signing.md as 'User-facing attestation signing and verification behavior', and docs/documentation-policy.md:14 requires external documentation to align with supported behavior.
advisory.finding: The new manifest-signing.md paragraph says rebar refuses, on POSIX, a provisioned REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH key that has any group or other permission bit. Only the op-cert service's startup composition (keyprov._read_path_source) enforces that. The general signing path, which this client page describes for `rebar sign`, rebar.sign_manifest, and the MCP sign_manifest tool, only checks that the override file exists. A 0644 key used through `rebar sign` is accepted, so the page misstates the behavior for its audience.
scenarios: A client on Linux points REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH at a 0644 key and runs `rebar sign`. The page says rebar refuses the key, but signing proceeds.
An operator reads the page and believes the CLI enforces key permissions, so they skip their own permission audit.
advisory.suggested_fix: Reword the first sentence of docs/manifest-signing.md:22 so it applies only to the op-cert service, for example: "On POSIX, the op-cert service refuses a provisioned `REBAR_OPCERT_KEY_PATH` file at startup if it has any group or other permission bit (it must be `0600` or stricter)." Keep the Windows residual-risk text, and phrase it as a skipped check in that same service path.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the `_write_new` symlink test fail when the `is_symlink()` guard is removed, e.g. check the error message or `__cause__`, or simulate an open that follows the link.
evidence: tests/unit/test_windows_mode_bit_skip.py:128: `(tmp_path / "real.json").unlink()  # dangling: O_EXCL alone would not see an existing file`

infra/scripts/cleanup_comment_echo_jira.py:312-313: `if path.is_symlink():  # portable counterpart of O_NOFOLLOW, absent on Windows` / `raise CleanupError(f"refusing to overwrite cleanup artifact: {path}")`

infra/scripts/cleanup_comment_echo_jira.py:315-325: flags include `os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL`, and `except FileExistsError as exc: raise CleanupError(f"refusing to overwrite cleanup artifact: {path}") from exc` gives the same message

POSIX open(2): when O_CREAT and O_EXCL are both set and the path is a symbolic link, open fails with EEXIST regardless of what the link points to, so the pre-existing O_EXCL path already refuses the dangling link

Named violating input: delete lines 312-313 (the added guard), then run `_write_new(<dangling symlink>, {"event": "x"})` with O_NOFOLLOW removed. It still raises CleanupError('refusing to overwrite cleanup artifact: ...') and real.json is still not created, so the test stays green
advisory.finding: test_a_symlink_is_never_overwritten_as_a_new_artifact still passes if the new `if path.is_symlink()` guard in `_write_new` is deleted. On POSIX, `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` on a dangling symlink fails with EEXIST whatever O_NOFOLLOW is set to. `_write_new` turns that FileExistsError into the same 'refusing to overwrite cleanup artifact' message the test matches, so the test cannot detect a regression in the added check on the Linux CI that gates. The test's comment 'O_EXCL alone would not see an existing file' is wrong for POSIX.
scenarios: A refactor drops the `is_symlink()` pre-check from `_write_new`. The Linux suite stays green, and the Windows-only protection this diff claims to add is no longer covered on the platform that gates.
advisory.suggested_fix: Tell the guard apart from the O_EXCL fallback. Either assert `excinfo.value.__cause__ is None` (the guard raises without chaining, while the FileExistsError path raises `from exc`), or monkeypatch `cleanup.os.open` to record any call and assert it was never called for the link path. Also fix or remove the comment that O_EXCL would not see the dangling link.

dropped.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the Windows symlink refusal atomic: lstat the path before os.open and refuse unless the fstat of the opened fd has the same (st_dev, st_ino), in _read_regular, _append_record and _write_new.
evidence: infra/scripts/cleanup_comment_echo_jira.py:173-174: comment says "O_NOFOLLOW does not exist on Windows, so refuse a symlink explicitly first; where the flag exists it still closes the check-then-open window". So the check-then-open window stays open where the flag is missing (Windows).

infra/scripts/cleanup_comment_echo_jira.py:175-179: `if path.is_symlink(): raise ...` then `flags = os.O_RDONLY | ... | getattr(os, "O_NOFOLLOW", 0)` then `descriptor = os.open(path, flags)`. Nothing ties the checked path to the opened file.
infra/scripts/cleanup_comment_echo_jira.py:183: `if not stat.S_ISREG(os.fstat(descriptor).st_mode)` runs fstat on the followed target, so a symlink pointing at a regular file passes.

infra/scripts/cleanup_comment_echo_jira.py:373-387: _append_record has the same is_symlink() check, then os.open(... O_CREAT | O_APPEND ...) and fstat S_ISREG. A link swapped in during the window gets the journal record appended to its target.
infra/scripts/cleanup_comment_echo_jira.py:312-323: _write_new has the same pattern for creating new artifacts.

infra/scripts/cleanup_comment_echo_jira.py:276: `if _POSIX_MODE_BITS and stat.S_IMODE(mode) & 0o077:` skips the group/world check on Windows, so nothing confirms other users cannot write into the directory where the swap would happen (docs/comment-echo-reclaim-runbook.md says 'nothing checks for extra entries such as Users or Everyone').
dropped.finding: On Windows, the new is_symlink() checks in _read_regular, _write_new and _append_record are check-then-open with nothing atomic behind them (O_NOFOLLOW resolves to 0). The fstat S_ISREG checks afterwards look at the file the open followed to. So if a symlink is swapped in between path.is_symlink() and os.open(), the script reads, creates or appends through it without noticing. The same change also removes the artifact-directory privacy check on Windows, which was the guarantee that no other user could write into the directory to do that swap.
scenarios: A Windows operator puts the artifact directory in a folder whose inherited ACL lets another local account write to it, and that account can create symlinks (Developer Mode or SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege). It replaces jira-before.json or the journal with a symlink between the check and the open. The script then reads attacker-chosen 'before' state, or appends journal records into a file the attacker picked.
dropped.suggested_fix: Record `pre = path.lstat()` (refuse if S_ISLNK), open the path, then `post = os.fstat(fd)`. Refuse and close the fd if `(post.st_dev, post.st_ino) != (pre.st_dev, pre.st_ino)` or the file is not S_ISREG. In _write_new, where the file does not exist yet, compare the fstat of the new fd with path.lstat() right after creation and refuse on a mismatch or if the path is now a symlink. On Windows st_ino is the NTFS file index, so the comparison works there.
